title: 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
description: President Donald Trump walks from the po
body:
President Donald Trump walks from the podium after speaking at a campaign rally at the Ocean Center, in Daytona Beach, Fla., Friday, Oct. 30, 2026.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/AP
    

   
   Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.   U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting.   When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.   
   The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.   Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them "fake news" and insults their journalists.   The White House did not immediately react publicly to Saturday's dismissal or respond to an AP request for comment.   Trump called the reporting 'malicious'   The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.   The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.   The letter bearing Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret," according to the newspaper.   
   Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory."   The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements," which, it alleged, caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president.   Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.   The lawsuit was dismissed once, then refiled   Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.   In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.   "The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Gayles wrote. "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."   The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimize Trump's denial, "Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it."   Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

title: Virginia and D.C. sue to block construction of Trump arch
description: A mockup of President Donald Trump's pro
body:
A mockup of President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch stands at the Great American State Fair on the National Mall, June 27, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jen Golbeck/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jen Golbeck/AP
    

   
   The commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit on Saturday to block construction on President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch.   The 45-page lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia called the project "flagrantly unlawful," attorneys general Jay Jones of Virginia and Brian Schwalb of the District of Columbia wrote.   
   The lawsuit is the latest legal attempt to stop construction of the 250-foot tall arch whose plans were unveiled by the Trump administration in Oct. 2025.   The attorneys general also allege that construction on the arch, which could begin as soon as next week, will "inflict irreparable harm" on the District and Virginia, including snarling traffic between both areas. The arch would be located between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. It would stand twice the height of the monument honoring America's 16th president.   
   "Both jurisdictions will need to take immediate and costly steps to assess, respond to, and mitigate these harmful effects," they wrote in the lawsuit. "These costs are severe and unrecoverable—particularly because Defendants have refused to take them into account or adequately consult with either jurisdiction during their hurried and preordained process to approve the Arch and start construction."   NPR reached out to both the White House and the Interior Department for comment on the lawsuit on Saturday but has not received a response.   Trump has previously defended plans to build the arch and said it would be a "military complex" to hold weapons and snipers.  The most recent plans for the arch, which will be reviewed by the National Capital Planning Commission, do not include military elements.   U.S. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkin ordered both sides to talk and to agree on a proposed briefing schedule on the motion for a temporary restraining order by Saturday evening.

title: What a midterm race in Kentucky says about how Democrats may do in Trump strongholds
description: Democrats are putting up a fight in midterm races this year that went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024. Kentucky Public Radi
body:
Democrats are putting up a fight in midterm races this year that went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024. Kentucky Public Radio's Sylvia Goodman explains what we can learn from one Kentucky district.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  The countdown to voting day is on. Candidates from both parties will be positioning and jockeying right up until Tuesday. Democrats are putting up a fight in states and districts this year that went for President Trump in 2024 by double digits. The president isn't on the ballot, but he knows that the control of Congress will shape the direction of the last two years of his term, so he's been riling his base in places he normally wouldn't land in midterm season, including Kentucky. So Kentucky Public Radio's capitol reporter Sylvia Goodman is with us to talk about a district that hasn't been competitive in almost a decade and is now rated a toss-up. Sylvia, this is the 6th Congressional District. Give us a sense of where it is and what its voting history is like.SYLVIA GOODMAN, BYLINE: Sure. Kentucky's 6th Congressional District is in the middle of the state, and it's our most purple district. It includes the bright-blue dot of Lexington but also includes a lot of suburbs and rural areas around it that tend to vote Republican. And in 2024, it voted for Trump by 15 points. However, just the year before, this same district voted for Democratic Governor Andy Beshear by 20 points. Democrats targeted this seat pretty early on. It's open this year, and Democrats have a chance to win in a district where Trump did so well.PFEIFFER: So in this open seat for Congress in Kentucky, who's running?GOODMAN: So on the right, there's Ralph Alvarado. He's Kentucky's first Hispanic state senator and he's formerly Tennessee's health commissioner. Alvarado got Trump's endorsement and ran with it during the primary. Since then, he's backed off from touting the president's support. He didn't go to Trump's northern Kentucky rally. He's backing away from tariffs. Alvarado initially supported the Iran war full-throatedly but now...RALPH ALVARADO: The president took action swiftly. We're now months into this conflict. We've got to have some resolution.GOODMAN: For the Democrats, there's Zach Dembo. He's a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor. He quit under the second Trump administration - he says because of the politicization of the DOJ. He's focused on his opposition to Trump policies, like the war tariffs and Medicaid cuts but also corruption.ZACH DEMBO: We're going to win this, but there are worse things than losing a campaign, like losing your integrity and going in bought and sold.GOODMAN: Like I said, the race has shifted around quite a bit. Both candidates seem to agree at this point - it's going to be a close one. Early voting has already started. Today is actually the last day of three here in Kentucky.PFEIFFER: Sylvia, I assume you've been out talking with voters. Give us a sense of what they're telling you.GOODMAN: Sure. I followed the campaign trails for Alvarado and Dembo last weekend. And the first thing in the morning, I went to this packed rally for Republicans in Lexington. There were, you know, candidates and volunteers mingling together. Some kind of scoffed at the idea of an enthusiasm gap for Republicans. Harry Van Epps (ph) told me that anyone who does their homework would vote for Alvarado in this race.HARRY VAN EPPS: You can't have open borders. You can't have Medicare for everyone. You know, it's called personal responsibility.GOODMAN: At a canvassing kickoff for Dembo later that day, Democrat Bobby McDowell (ph) from Scott County told me Dembo's really excited him.BOBBY MCDOWELL: And he's, you know, a former federal prosecutor, Navy JAG. He's got all the credentials. We haven't had a candidate like this in years.GOODMAN: Polls close in this district at 6 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, and it might be one of the first toss-ups in the country to get called on election night.PFEIFFER: Sylvia, this situation you're describing of seats that we wouldn't have thought would be competitive suddenly seeming competitive is not unique. And we've seen Democrats devoting a lot of resources and energy to these districts usually considered deep red. As we look at this district, what does it help us understand about whether the strategy is paying off for Democrats?GOODMAN: You know, Democrats have expanded the map quite a bit with competitive races in South Carolina, Iowa, Montana, Texas. Trump's approval rating is underwater. Kentucky has recorded the largest decline, actually, since January last year, falling 34 points to a negative 11 point net approval rating - that's per Civiqs polling. And Democrats are picking up on that frustration, and they're running with it. They're favored to flip the U.S. House of Representatives, and the Senate is in play this year too.PFEIFFER: That is Kentucky Public Radio's capitol reporter Sylvia Goodman. Thank you.GOODMAN: Thank you.

title: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe over Senate candidate
body:
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a campaign event Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, in Juneau, Alaska.
                
                    Chloe Anderson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chloe Anderson/AP
    

   
   ANCHORAGE, Alaska — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.   
   The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.   Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."   
   Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator. The owner of a boat dealership in the candidate's hometown of Petersburg who had donated to his campaign told The Associated Press that an FBI agent visited the business and wanted to know whether he had been misled by Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. He said he had not and that "Everybody knows who the incumbent is."   Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."   The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.   State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026.
                
                    Haven Daley/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Haven Daley/AP
    

   
   Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot: "I am not interested in tricking voters," she said.   
   Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest.   The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.   Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy "will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity."   "To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.   Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation would be possible, writing that voters' ballots are commingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.   They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.   Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska's ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.   
   Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael J. Heyman holds a news conference on a criminal investigation related to an alleged scheme to confuse voters by putting a Senate candidate on the ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent, at the James M. Fitzgerald U.S. Courthouse and Federal Building, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska.
                
                    Lindsey Wasson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Lindsey Wasson/AP
    

   
   Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.   It's highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.   Trump during a rally late Friday in Florida said Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan should be prosecuted. He noted U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche was in attendance and said, "He's going to make his own decision."   Trump, then addressing Blanche directly, said of decisions regarding the case, "Todd, please make your own," and watched Blanche's response.   Trump added: "OK, he said 'yes.'"   Peltola, at a campaign rally in Anchorage late Friday, said she is "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." She said she doesn't need any help in winning the race outside of the support of voters.   She was asked before the rally if it was possible that someone on her campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan: "I have no idea," she told KTUU. "I honestly have no idea."   The Times story revealing the potential recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan was based partly on interviews with a former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired before the August primary. Asked about Rios by the station, Peltola said certain people are "gone for a good reason. If I could fire them again, I'd be happy to fire them again."   
   Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.   Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.   
   Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.

title: The Healthcare Election: Florida
description: When federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health insurance expired last year, Florida was hit particularly hard. Now, as the election and
body:
When federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health insurance expired last year, Florida was hit particularly hard. Now, as the election and open enrollment coincide, healthcare is a major issue.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  When federal subsidies and Affordable Care Act healthcare plans expired last year, Florida was hit especially hard. This weekend, as open enrollment begins just days before Election Day, Floridians who use the healthcare exchange are learning what their new premiums are. On average, they're going up 10.4%, according to the state's Office of Insurance Regulation. NPR's Maham Javaid went to a competitive congressional district in Florida, spanning from the Gulf Coast to the suburbs of Palm Beach, to find out if rising healthcare insurance costs are moving votes.(SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING)MAHAM JAVAID, BYLINE: Bordering Naples Beach are palm trees and pastel-colored mansions. Brittany Garcia (ph), a 23-year-old registered nurse, is walking the shore after an overnight shift. Garcia has no health insurance.BRITTANY GARCIA: I would hope that there is some reform soon because I literally have no access to healthcare.JAVAID: She works as a contractor, so Garcia wants to buy insurance on the healthcare marketplace. Those are plans under the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. Premiums are rising as COVID-19-era subsidies have expired. For many like Garcia, healthcare has become unaffordable.GARCIA: I started looking and nothing was available, so I couldn't buy insurance. And to me, that was scary. You know, it made me think maybe I have to go to another country.JAVAID: Garcia has previously voted Republican. Now, without access to insurance, she's not sure how she will vote.GARCIA: This time, I'm just voting with my convictions.JAVAID: The newly redrawn 22nd Congressional District sprawls across south Florida. Made up of rural, urban and suburban areas, it's home to wealthy communities and working-class families. Politically, it swings between red and blue. Northeast of Naples, Collier County is a diverse area, home to immigrants from Haiti, Mexico and Guatemala. This is where Bianca (ph) and her husband live. They've been without insurance since January. That's when her insurance agent called and said...BIANCA: But I do want to let you know that because they're going to take away the subsidy, that it's now going to be this amount of money. And at the time, I think it was, like, doubled or tripled of what we were paying.JAVAID: She's had to pay out of pocket for an emergency visit to the hospital and pneumonia treatment. Bianca asked NPR not to use her full name because political activists in her community have faced harassment for speaking up. She's going to vote for the Democratic nominee, Pia Dandiya, and her reason is healthcare.BIANCA: She is trying to expand the Affordable Care Act, which I think is really important, especially for, like, families like mine and my husband, where we're working 40 hours a week, and we can't afford healthcare.JAVAID: Nice to meet you.ROHIT DANDIYA: Nice to meet you. I'm Pia's father.JAVAID: On the western edge of the district, Dandiya's father welcomes us into her campaign office.R DANDIYA: Here. Come on in. Hello. Pia, are you here?PIA DANDIYA: Hey, Dad.R DANDIYA: They're here.P DANDIYA: Amazing. Come on in.JAVAID: If Democrats were to win back the House, Dandiya says she's going to work on restoring ACA subsidies, expanding funding to Medicaid and lowering drug prices.P DANDIYA: Healthcare is not a blue issue or a red issue. It's a red, white and blue issue. It's something that is impacting all of us.JAVAID: Her Republican opponent, Casey Askar, wants to eliminate the ACA altogether and crack down on fraud to preserve Medicare and Medicaid. His campaign did not reply to interview requests.The district is home to many retirees and veterans who often vote for Republicans. Several of those we spoke to express satisfaction with the healthcare options they already have, including Medicare and private insurance. But Dandiya says the district she's running in doesn't lean either way.R DANDIYA: This district is actually a microcosm of our country's politics, that it is truly purple, and voters are just trying to find a way to make their ends meet.JAVAID: Deep in the Everglades that span the district, besides the swamps, you'll also find sugarcane fields, cattle farms and people picking up their groceries at the Dollar General.(SOUNDBITE OF CAR STARTING)JAVAID: Deanna Johnson (ph) is one of them. The 24-year-old dental hygiene student has been looking for insurance plans on the marketplace.DEANNA JOHNSON: We're kind of in the middle of trying to get health insurance 'cause currently, everything is so high now.JAVAID: She says her family is feeling the affordability crisis. They had to move inland from West Palm Beach when rent got too high. She's hoping things get better in the future.JOHNSON: I hope we get free healthcare like you know, in other countries. They get free healthcare.JAVAID: Johnson is the kind of swing voter candidates will need to win here.JOHNSON: I voted for the red last time, but this time, now I'm thinking about voting blue to get our country back in order.(SOUNDBITE OF CAR STARTING)JAVAID: At an early voting site in the suburb of Sunrise, Brent Harris (ph), a 58-year-old who works in construction, is thinking about...BRENT HARRIS: Democracy, corruption, how people are treated. Then, of course, there's healthcare, immigration. I'm really, really not happy with the way things are.JAVAID: He voted for President Trump in 2016. This year, he's voting for the Democrats. Harris worries about insurance for his family. One of his daughters is on Medicaid, but her 1-month-old daughter is uninsured. Two other adult kids working multiple jobs can't afford insurance. Harris thinks healthcare is a bipartisan problem.HARRIS: But I think working together collectively is hopefully going to be solved.JAVAID: For voters like Harris, in this affordability election, healthcare is just one more way the math has stopped working.Maham Javaid, NPR News, Broward County, Florida.

title: Supreme Court hears religious freedom case centered on universal pre-K program
description: A view of the Supreme Court in Washingto
body:
A view of the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 14.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   On Tuesday, the Supreme Court hears arguments in a case that pits the Catholic Church against taxpayer funded school programs for all 4-year-olds in Colorado. At issue is whether religious schools may refuse to admit the children of gay and trans parents in violation of a state law that bars discrimination.   The first line of the Bill of Rights says: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." As early as the founding of this country, Thomas Jefferson described the clause as creating a "wall of separation between church and state."   
   The Supreme Court formally embraced that idea in the 1940s, making it the law of the land — until roughly 10 years ago. That's when the court's new conservative majority made an increasingly dramatic doctrinal U-turn, focusing not on the separation of church and state, but on that second clause in the First Amendment: protecting the free exercise of religion.   "It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago. It is just a complete shift," says Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch, who has written extensively about the Constitution's religion clauses.   To cite just one example, the Supreme Court, by an 8-to-1 vote, ruled in 1983 that that Bob Jones University should lose its tax exempt status because it prohibited interracial dating and interracial marriage on religious grounds, and that constitutes racial discrimination that the government money may not support.   That said, it's unclear if the court will reach a similar conclusion now.    Why is that? Because race has a "unique" place in U.S. history, contends professor Douglas Laycock, emeritus professor of law at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Virginia. "There's nothing like 250 years of slavery, civil war, 750,000 dead, three constitutional amendments. Nothing like that for any other group," he says.   
   As for the Colorado case, Laycock acknowledges that the Denver archdiocese is discriminating, but he adds, "The question is whether that discrimination is a protected exercise of religion." Rather than focusing on separation of church and state, the current court instead has focused on the rights of religious groups when pitted against state and federal laws that ban discrimination based on race, sex, religion or other categories.   It's the sex part that has thrown a monkey wrench into Colorado's broad program aimed at ensuring that virtually all 4-year-olds in the state get a pre-K education.   "The law really was about implementing a program that said we want every kid, no matter where you live, to be able to have access to universal preschool," says Steve Fenberg, who served as president of the Colorado state Senate when the pre-k program was enacted, complete with a $6,300 benefit for each child enrolled in the program every year, money that comes from a tobacco tax.   To accomplish that, the state did something most other states have not. It created a broad plan, including religious schools, as long as the schools abide by a state law that bars discrimination based on race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.   
   Colorado state Rep. Emily Sirota, a prime sponsor of the universal pre-K bill, emphasizes that the state wanted parents to have "a robust choice" about where their 4-year-olds would go to school.   Indeed, she notes that the Catholic Church initially endorsed the program, and Catholic Charities continues to participate, along with other religious groups, including at least 35 Christian schools, one Muslim and three Jewish schools.   "The caveat is that you can't discriminate, and you need to allow all students to participate," says former state Sen. Fenberg.   That caveat is where things went awry. The Denver Archdiocese and two parishes challenged the law in court, represented by the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty and its CEO, Mark Rienzi. He maintains that the Colorado law flatly discriminates against Catholic schools.   
   "They're only excluding religious schools that are organized around beliefs that Colorado doesn't like. And that's the constitutional problem," says Rienzi. "Not everybody has to be Catholic to show up, but they do have to agree to support Catholic teachings and not publicly contradict Catholic teachings. That's the way these schools are set up."   Therefore, the church wants an exemption from the state's anti-discrimination law, which makes it illegal to refuse entrance to school for 4-year-olds whose parents or potentially other family members are gay or trans.   
   Of course, not all Catholic programs march to the same drummer.   "I don't agree with the sky is falling," says Tim Uhl, who has held multiple leadership positions for Catholic school systems in seven states. He is currently the interim director of mission and ministry at Notre Dame High School in San Jose, Calif., and is among a group of Catholic school directors who has filed a brief siding with Colorado.   "We do admit students that are not Catholic and families that are not Catholic," Uhl notes, adding that non-Catholic families "understand that even if they don't agree with certain doctrine, that doesn't mean they're going to be disruptive … You know, diversity of opinion and diversity of thought is part of an educational experience."   But the archdiocese of Denver has a different viewpoint. In an article published in the Denver Post, Archbishop James R. Golka wrote that as a result of the Colorado pre-K program, enrollment in Catholic schools is down 20% across the archdiocese and two preschools have closed, including one which serves "minority and low income families."   But the larger "tragedy," said the archbishop, is that "Colorado's attack on Catholic education threatens the broader culture. In our age of hyper- secularization, moral relativism, and technical reductionism, we urgently need schools that teach students who they truly are: immortal souls, beloved by God." Instead, he added, "The predictable result is a culture unmoored from truth, adrift in confusion."   
   Scott Elmer, superintendent of Catholic schools for the Archdiocese, says "it's very rare" for LGBTQ parents to try to enroll their children. "This is not something we deal with regularly," he adds.   That said, however, the Supreme Court's conservative supermajority, including President Trump's three appointees, have sent strong signals that they are headed toward revolutionizing religious rights in ways not widely embraced before.   Last year, the court was evenly divided as to whether taxpayer-funded charter schools could include religious schools and teachings. But because Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself over a potential conflict of interest, the justices dropped the case.   
   Now, the Colorado case is before the Supreme Court, and this time Barrett has not felt a necessity to recuse. So there will be a full court ready to decide the case.   "The question is, how far will the Supreme Court go in requiring the government to pay for religious schools?" asks Berkeley Law School dean Erwin Chemerinsky.   Then too, he observes, "there's the issue of will the government have to fund religious charter schools? … We don't know how far the court's willing to go." After all, charter schools were designed to be public schools that operate independently under a performance-based contract with state or local government agencies that provide taxpayer money for funding.   
   There are some 8,000 charter schools nationally, and roughly 276 in Colorado, and they have not, until now, been run by religious groups.   Just a few weeks ago, however, a federal district judge in Oklahoma allowed a taxpayer-funded Jewish charter school "grounded in enduring Jewish values" to open, using $2.6 million in state funding that is projected to grow to $8.3 million in state funds by 2030. The fate of the school remains in limbo.    Whether that continues and expands depends, of course, on the Supreme Court's decision in the Colorado case.

schema.headline: Supreme Court hears religious freedom case centered on universal pre-K program

title: Trump thanks supporters for the memories in final campaign stops for 2026 midterms
description: President Donald Trump gestures during a
body:
President Donald Trump gestures during a campaign rally at the Rock Hill Sports and Event Center on October 29, 2026 in Rock Hill, South Carolina.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      President Trump was comparing his 2016 campaign rally size to the rallies Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders was having that year, when the president took a detour.   "We have the biggest rallies ever in history," Trump said, turning from braggadocious to reflective. "I hope you enjoy it because you're never going to see it again. You will never see what we've done. You'll never see it happen again."   Trump was in South Carolina to boost two Senate candidates who he personally picked but who have struggled to ignite excitement among Republican voters: Darline Graham in South Carolina and Michael Whatley in North Carolina.   
   This was one of Trump's final rallies after a flurry of midterm campaign events over the past month. More than 25 rallies in October alone, mostly in red states where Republicans are facing serious political headwinds. The official purpose is to help those Republicans win their races, but for a president whose trademark has always been big raucous rallies, there was more to it.   Trump won't be on the ballot again and once these midterms are over, it's not clear how many Republican candidates will want voters pretending he is. Right now, though, that is his plea.   "Please pretend I'm on the ballot cause in a way I am on the ballot, because they want to do away with all of the tremendous things we've done. The tax cuts, the border," Trump said last week at a rally in Greenville, N.C.   Like any performer on what could be a farewell tour, Trump plays a lot of the greatest hits. He has a regular riff about tariffs.   "Tariffs. The tariffs. My favorite word," Trump said in Lubbock, Tex. "I always say it, but I had to change it to fifth favorite. You've heard me say this. I said it's my favorite word. It's made us rich."    
   But there are also new ones, like the instant classic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted's butt, which, once Trump got a laugh, he just kept repeating everywhere he went.   "So, I'm studying him and I made the mistake of saying that I started off by studying his ass," Trump said. "I just wanted to see."   This wasn't just a key pitch in Ohio, where perhaps some voters could be persuaded by the idea of a senator with a well built behind.   "The audience loved it. By the way, [Husted] went up 12 points that day," Trump said confidently despite evidence to the contrary. "He went from being down to being up."   He even talked about Husted's butt in Texas, where Trump's reviews of Senate candidate Ken Paxton's looks have been less complimentary.   "Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton, but I'm not sure your body is going to qualify," Trump said to laughs.   As a closing argument, Trump's message is unconventional at best. Unhelpful may be a better description. Even the $5,000 "Trump dividend" he's promising to all American adults if Republicans win the House and the Senate comes with an off message weave.   "You'll be my guest at Mar-a-Lago," Trump mused. "The problem is that for $5000, the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert. I'm not even sure you could buy that."   Trump added that Mar-a-Lago, his Florida resort, isn't a great place for the cost conscious.   In a year when affordability is a top issue, this is a performance for the Trump faithful, who eat it up.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Blake Marnell, wearing a suit with a pattern similar to bricks, is seen as President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, North Carolina, on October 20, 2026.
                
                    Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Blake Marnell is often one of the first people through the gates at Trump's rallies. He's from San Diego, but was in Greenville, NC for Trump's rally there.   "I took the month of October off thinking that there would be a few rallies as it turned out there's a ton of them," Marnell said. "I'm just going from rally to rally. Some people like to go on cruises. I like political rallies."   
   Marnell isn't just any Trump fan. He's famous for his dedication, always in the front row, wearing a suit meant to be an homage to Trump's early campaign promise to build the wall. His alter ego is "Brick Suit."   "But President Trump calls me Mr. Wall," Marnell said.   Shouting out "Mr. Wall" is a regular feature of a Trump rally, along with the "Front Row Joe's" and "the lovely ladies from North Carolina." It's all part of the show.   
   Marnell is certain Trump will hold more rallies leading up to the 2028 presidential election, but he says these midterm rallies have felt different than when Trump actually was on the ballot.   Cindy New, from Emerald Isle, North Carolina said she voted for Trump three times, but had never seen him live. Heading into the Greenville rally, she said she was just hoping for a good show.   "He can't run again, they say, so I guess I gotta come while he gets close," New said. "I missed all the rest of them, so I gotta come see him once. I don't need to do it but once. One and done."   Trump's rally that night featured an Air Force One fly over and a nearly two hour speech from the president — the full experience.   In Fort Myers, Fla., Valerie Thivierge showed up bedazzled. She hadn't been to a Trump rally before either, despite owning a store in town that is devoted to him. She closed her store for the rally "of course."   "This is our life. This is what we do all year long and I want to see him," Thivierge said.   By Trump's telling, the people are why he keeps holding rallies. At a recent event in the Oval Office, he said it isn't easy standing up there for two hours "ranting and raving."   
   "You have the crowds," Trump said. "There's a lot of love in those rooms."   On Thursday, the Republican National Committee announced Trump would be canceling two weekend rallies that had been planned for Iowa and Kansas. Instead, they said, he would be holding a series of tele-rallies, a way to reach the party faithful more efficiently with just days left until the end of voting.   Less than 24 hours later, the in-person rallies were back, now both scheduled for Sunday.   "President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday," said a source familiar with the scheduling change who wasn't authorized to speak on the record.   Trump's time at the center of the political universe is ticking down, but he keeps playing the hits. And the most loyal fans keep coming.   "We've been doing this together for 11 years and there's never been anything like it and there probably never will be anything like it again, politically or otherwise," Trump said as he closed out a rally in Corpus Christi, Tex. "So let's go out and do what we do best. Let's win on November 3rd. We've got to win."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Trump dances to music as he arrives for a campaign rally on October 30, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Fla.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   There's fondness in these final days but also exhaustion, especially as the president faces down an election that might not go well for his party. Friday night in Daytona Beach, Fla., at what would have been his last rally, Trump blended bitterness with nostalgia.   "I thought this was it. I thought I could relax. 28 days in a row of this crap is a lot. It's a lot," Trump said.   "My voice is operating at about 49.2%," he added.

schema.headline: Trump thanks supporters for the memories in final campaign stops for 2026 midterms

title: Here's how to watch election night as the polls close, hour-by-hour
description: People grab stickers on the first day of
body:
People grab stickers on the first day of early voting in New York, on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.
                
                    Heather Khalifa/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Heather Khalifa/AP
    

   
   Vote counting will start Tuesday night but could go on for days or even weeks.   While control of the House could become clear sooner because of bigger margins, control of the Senate could take much longer — the margins are tighter, seven states are especially competitive and two states use ranked choice voting which can prolong count time. Control of the House likely won't come down to one seat, but control of the Senate very well could.   As results are being tallied, here is a guide to watch election night as polls close across the country (all times in Eastern Time and organized by latest poll close time).       
   To jump to a specific poll closing time, use the links below:7 p.m. ET | 7:30 p.m. ET | 8 p.m. ET | 8:30 p.m. ET | 9 p.m. ET | 10 p.m. ET | 11 p.m. ET | 12 a.m. ET | 1 a.m. ET      7 p.m. ET: Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Virginia, Vermont   To get things started, all eyes are on the senate and gubernatorial races in Georgia and Florida.   
   Georgia: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is likely to defeat Republican Rep. Mike Collins in the race for Senate. The governor's race is tighter, one of the most competitive in the south between Republican nominee, billionaire businessman Rick Jackson and Democratic candidate, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Despite delays in elections past, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger has told local news that new laws require counties to report results within an hour of polls closing.    South Carolina: This is an unexpectedly tight Senate race between Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after her brother Linsdey Graham died, and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. Many national polls say the race in this heavily Republican state is a toss up, while the Cook Political Report says Republicans have the advantage.   7:30 p.m. ET: North Carolina, Ohio, West Virginia   North Carolina and Ohio have Senate and governor's races to watch.   
   North Carolina: Polls and pundits show North Carolina's Republican-held Senate seat is the most likely flip for the Democrats. The contest is between former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and close Trump ally. The last time Democrats won a Senate race in the state was in 2008, and the path to a Democratic majority becomes much less likely if the party loses this one.    
   Ohio: This is the first of the seven tight Senate races on Tuesday night that could define control of the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown are deadlocked. Ohio used to be thought of as a swing state but in the last decade, it's become solidly Republican, so the close races have attracted attention. For governor, former state health director, Democrat Amy Acton is leading in the polls against venture capitalist, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who recently launched an attack ad against Acton featuring her estranged mother. The blowback to the ad was so significant, it could hurt Husted as well as Ramaswamy.   8 p.m.: Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Washington, D.C.   Polls would now be closed in more than half the country. There is potential for calls at poll-close in governor's races in favor of Republicans in Alabama, South Dakota and Tennessee and in favor of Democrats in Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maine, Maryland, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island.   Maine: Despite the late entry by the Democratic candidate, Troy Jackson, the race is tough for incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But Collins has remained resilient in face of challenges in the past. This is another seat targeted by Democrats to pick up, in the only place a Republican holds a Senate seat in a state won by Kamala Harris in 2024.    
   Florida: Another former swing state that has become solidly red in recent elections, the governor's race between Republican Rep. Byron Donalds and his Democratic opponent David Jolly favors Republicans. But for Donalds to hold only a slight poll advantage follows the national trend of Republicans lagging behind in traditional strongholds. The Senate race is slightly less competitive. Incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody is poised to win over Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon. Where Florida has a lot of political consequence on election night is in its competitive House races. Florida is a state that redrew its congressional maps ahead of this election and this will be the first test. According to the Cook Political Report, seven House seats are competitive with two toss-ups.   Pennsylvania: For a significant portion of this election cycle, Pennsylvania has been the state with the most competitive House races — four, including three toss-ups. But as the map has solidified in the last month, all three toss-ups now lean toward Democrats. The last is a toss-up. Democrats could have a big night here.   New Hampshire: At one point, this race was quite close but the gap between Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former Republican Sen. John Sununu has widened, giving Pappas the edge. Still, New Hampshire is a state with a popular Republican governor expected to win in the same election and Republicans see this as a potential long-shot pick up opportunity.   8:30 p.m.: Arkansas   Arkansas: The Senate race is not very competitive but if Republicans' margin is smaller than usual, that could show that Democrats got more votes than usual in places that they haven't traditionally won. Plus, there's a House race here that Republicans have poured money into in the final days. Not a state to watch closely but could give insight into the larger electorate.   
   9 p.m.: Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Wisconsin and Wyoming   Another major hour for poll closures. At this point, polls are closed in more than 80% of the states. Eyes and energy will begin shifting to initial results out of Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Texas, where competitive senate races are at play that could decide control of the chamber.   Arizona: One of the most competitive gubernatorial contests is happening in this swing state. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs is hoping to fend off MAGA-aligned Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. This has tilted toward Hobbs at the end but Arizona is known for an independent streak in politics.   There are major Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Texas. Three of those states are reliably Republican and Democrats' ability to be neck-and-neck in those states shows the frustration voters feel about the economy and the Trump presidency.   
   In Texas, a Democrat hasn't won statewide since the early 1990s. Democratic nominee state Rep. James Talarico faces off against Republican nominee Ken Paxton, who has had to grapple with a scandal-riddled past. Talarico could take an early lead as early voting data and mail in ballots are counted but Paxton will probably start to gain ground as counties will start reporting their totals. While the governor's race between Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa is also close, Abbott is still favored.    Kansas Republicans are trying to keep Sen. Roger Marshall in the Senate. This seemed like a safe seat for Republicans until Democrat Adam Hamilton entered with his moderate message. Add to that, the Trump brand is not having the same impact in Kansas as it once did and we have another race that's become too close to call.   Republicans are nervous about Iowa because the open Senate race is a little too close for comfort. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is up against Democratic moderate state Rep. Josh Turek. Plus, three of the state's four Republican-held congressional seats are competitive, with two leaning toward Democrats. Democrats have their strongest chance for a pick up at governor in Iowa with state auditor Rob Sand. He's favored after running a very strong campaign, deemphasizing partisan politics.   
   A lot of media oxygen this election cycle focused on Michigan as the race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers unfolded. Republicans spent money running Islamophobic ads against El-Sayed who responded by leaning deeper into his personal story. Tuesday night will reveal which struck a chord with Michiganders. If El-Sayed wins, it will be a massive victory for the progressive wing of the party but this race remains a toss-up, even as the swing state's governor contest favors the Democrat, secretary of state Jocelyn Benson over Republican Rep. John James.   Then there's Minnesota, which, like New Hampshire, is a long-shot pick up target for Republicans. What's different here is that Democrats nominated progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan who has had to answer questions about fraud in state agencies that happened under her watch. Plus, Republican candidate, former NFL sportscaster Michelle Tafoya has run a solid race and been able to toe the line between distancing from Trump and backing Republican policies. Tafoya isn't expected to win but Minnesota could be too close for comfort for Democrats.   There are many competitive House races in this time block, including toss up races in Arizona, Colorado, Michigan and New York. With such a narrow majority for Republicans in the chamber, each of these races will be closely watched to see which seats Democrats are able to flip.   10 p.m. Montana, Nevada, Utah   Polls in three more mountain west states are closed. Eyes are on Montana, another reliably Republican state, that could surprise the country by sending a Democrat to Congress.   Montana: The state's closest race is the toss-up House race in the 1st Congressional District where Sam Forstag, the Democratic nominee and former smokejumper, and Republican Aaron Flint, a combat veteran, are in a competitive race. Another interesting race in Montana is the Senate contest. The independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, feels like he has a shot at winning the race against a Republican incumbent and a Democrat who is on the ballot but Republicans are favored.   
   Nevada: Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is fighting to keep his seat in a state that has been hit hard by economic conditions. Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford is the Democratic nominee and the race is considered a toss-up.   11 p.m.: California, Idaho, Oregon, Washington   At this point, voters in the Pacific Northwest, California and Idaho are done casting ballots. It could feel like a whole new election night has begun.    
   California: The state has a new congressional map affecting the state of some House races. In 2025, voters opted to redraw the boundaries in the state in response to President Trump's redistricting battle to secure more safe Republican seats. The decision made the state less competitive for Republicans and the close races have mostly tilted toward Democrats in the final weeks. But in California's Central Valley, there is a true toss-up race. There are also tax-related propositions on California's ballot, including a billionaire tax. California is a slow counting state so races may not be called quickly.   Oregon: Despite Oregon being a solidly blue state, voters are unhappy with the Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek. She faces a closer than expected race against Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan.   12 a.m. ET: Hawaii 1 a.m. ET: Alaska    Alaska: The final state to finish voting on Election Day and by this point in the night (early Wednesday morning on the East Coast), people will be eagerly awaiting the first drop of results for the toss-up Senate race. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is in a race against Democratic nominee, former Rep. Mary Peltola. But there's been some drama in the contest. There are two Dan Sullivans in the ballet. A recent investigation by the New York Times alleges the Democratic party may have recruited the other Dan Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent Dan Sullivan. Peltola denies any involvement in the alleged scheme.    
   The governor's race is also competitive, with three Republican candidates on the ballot and one Democrat. That Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, picked up a key endorsement from Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski. The other statewide race, Alaska's at-large congressional seat, is leaning toward Republicans but still less competitive than in past years. A note of caution: Alaska uses ranked choice voting and the results could take weeks — yes, weeks — to be finalized.

title: Election officials worry about DOJ monitoring of Tuesday's vote
description: Some election officials have been notified that the DOJ will be monitoring their polling stations. NPR's voting correspondent Miles Parks expla
body:
Some election officials have been notified that the DOJ will be monitoring their polling stations. NPR's voting correspondent Miles Parks explains what he's watching for on election day - and afterwards.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  A federal judge has ordered the Justice Department not to threaten election workers who are processing the ballots of people the federal government claims are ineligible to vote. That comes as many election officials nationwide say the federal government is undermining trust in voting procedures. NPR voting correspondent Miles Parks recently got a tip that helped him break a story about the Justice Department notifying places it wants to monitor on Election Day. Like any good beat reporter, he followed it up.MILES PARKS, BYLINE: We had confirmed about 15 different counties who had received them, like you mentioned, in blue, red and purple places. So we were starting to get - and that list seemed to be growing in real time.PFEIFFER: When I sat down to speak with Miles for our weekly Reporter's Notebook, he said that, although the DOJ sends monitors out in every election, this year, it feels different.PARKS: We've seen the Department of Justice take a number of unprecedented actions during Trump's second term, whether that is suing states trying to access their sensitive voter data, whether it is the president putting executive actions out there that have been struck down by courts for overreaching his authority. And so when you take all of that as the landscape, the idea that the DOJ would be coming - if you're a county voting official, the DOJ coming to your voting locations, it makes you a little bit more uneasy. But it also makes - what I kept hearing from voting officials is that they were hearing from voters that they were nervous.PFEIFFER: We mentioned that you were the first to report on some of these notices going out. If you can share how you found that out - are they not made public, and you started to hear from election clerks that these notices were showing up?PARKS: I got a call from an election official who said, we got a notice, and people here are freaking out. I can't name the election official who first told me that, but I basically emailed and called every election official I know and every person who knows election officials in the country, and just said, I'm hearing these are going out. Have you gotten one, or do you know of anyone who has gotten one of these? And so what that allowed us to do is, A, get a sense of the places that they were going, but more importantly, was talk to the election officials in those places and hear how these requests were being perceived.PFEIFFER: And in terms of how the requests are being perceived, you had one election clerk, a Democrat, actually say to you on the record that they think it's politically motivated and potentially an intimidation technique. Do they feel like there's a risk to saying that out loud, that they might invite more scrutiny from the administration?PARKS: I did hear that, and I heard that from a lot of people on background and off the record, as well, who - everyone is very nervous right now to basically get - to be under the scrutiny of the Trump administration. I think we've seen in previous election cycles - 2020 comes to mind - what happens in places like Georgia and Michigan and Arizona, whether it is the death threats that come from that, the political pressure that comes from that if you are an election official in one of these places where the Trump campaign or people who are spreading misinformation around elections are focused. And so, yes, I think there is kind of the underlying fear.I think this election official knew that it was going to be public that the DOJ was coming to his county and so made the calculated decision to talk with us, and I appreciated that. And I think what was so interesting is he had this situation where the neighboring clerk, who was a Republican, did not receive one of these monitoring notifications. And so...PFEIFFER: This is interesting. Is this the one - 'cause I went back and read your story - where one of the counties was heavily Latino population, so they have a rule where they provide Spanish language ballots...PARKS: Exactly.PFEIFFER: ...And the other doesn't?PARKS: Exactly. There's a specific provision in the Voting Rights Act that says if a certain percentage of your population is of different ethnicities or different races, based on the U.S. census, then you may be required to provide ballot materials. And so the DOJ is saying we're going to this county because we're interested in enforcing this specific aspect of the Voting Rights Act. Though, I think a lot of election officials, when you tell them that, and that election official in that county, was not comforted by that because this DOJ has not shown any previous interest in enforcing ballot protections for people who speak Spanish.PFEIFFER: So the DOJ might be saying on the surface, we're just going to make sure everybody gets their Spanish ballot. The clerks are afraid they're going to show up to try to scrutinize, maybe detain Latinos.PARKS: Exactly. And I think, again, they're - as you mentioned, this same DOJ sent monitors during the primary to close to a dozen states, and on a whole, that was uneventful, that many states who had these monitors at their polling places and at their election offices found no issues. I will say, though, there was one incident in Wyoming where the Republican governor there and the Republican clerk there said there were monitors who were, quote, "aggressive," who did not seem to show a respect for state law around elections. And so, at the same time, I would say, broadly speaking, the election officials I'm talking to are expecting this monitoring effort to go somewhat as normal, but I just think that they're on higher alert than they ever have been about this effort.PFEIFFER: And are you hearing from the clerks that they have a variety of fears? I mean, one is that a voter shows up and gets detained. One is that voters may not bother to show up and vote because they're afraid of showing up and getting detained. So what's the universe of worries these clerks have about what could play out on Election Day?PARKS: The one concern that rises above all else goes back to federal law enforcement, goes back to the Department of Justice - not about this monitoring effort, necessarily, but about the idea of ballot seizures and the idea that federal law enforcement could get a search warrant to be able to take possession of ballots. This is something that was not on the radar of local election officials until this year, when the FBI served a search warrant in Fulton County, Georgia, which was an area that really was an epicenter for conspiracy theories around the 2020 election. The ballots being seized out of that elections office there was really unprecedented.PFEIFFER: And remind me - that happened after the election? They came in and said, we want all your paperwork.PARKS: Exactly. Many years after the election - they basically said, we're investigating crimes around recordkeeping, and so they confiscated all these ballots. But even that idea, the idea that federal law enforcement could confiscate ballots or election materials in the way they did, was pretty unprecedented. And so it just opened up a lot of these clerks' eyes of, like, what happens if it's November 5, and we haven't even finished counting it? We haven't even finished - you know, we're still getting absentee ballots that were postmarked but haven't been counted yet. You know, there - we're still kind of in the thick of it of trying to determine how many votes we have at all, and we get a knock on the door, and it's federal law enforcement, and they're saying we have a signed search warrant, and we're able to seize X number of ballots. Again, it's an outlandish scenario, but it's one that I can tell you election officials across the country have been preparing for all year.PFEIFFER: I was going to say - I'm sure many of them would say it's not that outlandish.PARKS: Feels less outlandish now than it ever has before.PFEIFFER: Were the same issues at play when you first began and now it's just gotten more and more intense over the decade? Or are you actually seeing new things now that you never saw and couldn't have imagined seeing when you started this beat?PARKS: Definitely, the latter. And I think what has been so interesting about covering this beat the last few election cycles is that every election has had actually a different sort of red blinking light concern. When I think of the post-2016 election cycle - after the Russian election interference in 2016 - for four years, everyone was talking about cybersecurity. Just the idea of foreign election interference, trying to make sure we - you know, we had not been spending a lot of time thinking about hardening our systems until that moment - was a real wake-up call where counties everywhere were thinking about cybersecurity in a new way.After 2020, it was physical security and all the threats that came from, you know, that intense, intense period that led up to January 6. After 2024, it has been how to interact with a federal government that is being helmed by a person who does not believe elections are legitimate. And that has just raised a whole slew of new questions election officials have never interacted with before.PFEIFFER: We obviously don't know how the election will play out. Maybe the election monitoring will go perfectly fine. But if you are still covering this beat four years from now in the next election, any way for you to forecast where we're headed, what we might see that's the new iteration of this in four years?PARKS: Honestly, the thing I'm most curious about is this brand of election denial that President Trump has been kind of seeding in the American public for 10 years. Where does that go from here, and specifically, among Democrats? I think we're at a point right now where - and again, at this point, election - I want to be very clear that election denial is being propped up on the right. But when you ask polling questions about how people feel about election results, because of all the fears about the federal government, there are a lot of people on the left who feel that if Republicans win this midterm election, it will be because of some sort of fraud or malfeasance.And it's very possible that that is not the case, that Republicans - you know, this is going to be a very tightly contested election in the House, in the U.S. Senate. And so when the entire American electorate is feeling as cynical and as scared and as existential as they are right now, I think it would be naive to think that this level of distrust is going to continue to be isolated among a small portion of Republicans.PFEIFFER: On Election Day, Miles, there are so many places you could go. Will you go somewhere physically? Will you just work the phones? What are you going to do on Election Day?PARKS: I will be here at NPR headquarters, probably for 24 straight hours. And then my plan is, on the day after the election - Wednesday afternoon and Wednesday night - we should have a better sense of the places that are still contested, and that will be where I head.PFEIFFER: I hope we'll be able to have you back on the show after you visited some of those election sites, and you can tell us what you saw and how this played out.PARKS: Always happy to do it, Sacha.PFEIFFER: That is NPR's Miles Parks. Thank you.PARKS: Thank you.

      Accuracy and availability of transcripts for NPR programming may vary. Transcript text may also be revised to correct errors or match updates to audio. Audio may be edited after its original broadcast or publication. The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.
      
      Please note that NPR platforms and products also include some programming produced by third parties; NPR cannot guarantee transcripts for that content and some transcripts may be produced using automated or other tools.

title: What's it like to run for Congress when the odds are stacked heavily against you?
body:
Democratic congressional hopeful Lisa Kinney campaigns at Johnny J's Diner in Casper, Wyo. on October 19, 2026.
                
                    Natalie Behring for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Natalie Behring for NPR
    

   
   Much ink has been spilled this election cycle about the competitive races that could determine which party controls Congress.   But tossup districts represent only a fraction of congressional races. The vast majority — 80% — are rated solid Republican or solid Democrat. Candidates running against the political grain face an uphill battle, with campaigns marked by limited resources, dwindling donors, and scarce staff.   What's it like to run for Congress when political wisdom says you'll probably lose?   It's a question Lisa Kinney has heard again and again.   She's running as a Democrat for the lone House seat in Wyoming. Since the late 1970s, it has only sent Republicans to Congress.   
   "I don't think the people of Wyoming always hear both sides," Kinney says during a day of campaigning in Casper. "I'm glad to give another opinion. And I'm a Wyomingite, so I'm still moderate no matter what."   
   You wouldn't know it from an ad from her opponent that places her next to progressive figures Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.   Kinney says she finds it funny, albeit bemusing.   "What's he thinking — that we all get together and do socialist stuff?" she chuckles as she walks into Johnny J's to talk to early risers.   After perusing the pecan and cinnamon rolls, Kinney makes her way through the crowded diner. She's met with some hasty "nopes" from people who want to keep politics away from their pancakes — along with a gentleman who says he can't support a party that doesn't back Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a woman who doesn't like Democrats' stance on trans issues.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Hunter Svejkovsky brought his horses out shopping in Casper, Wyo. "With the price of diesel right now, it's a lot cheaper," he said. Svejkovsky said he's not very politically active, but took a card from Lisa Kinney, who's running for the sole U.S. House seat in the state.
                
                    Natalie Behring for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Natalie Behring for NPR
    

   
   Then she meets Joe Beck, who doesn't identify with either party. He says he's fed up with the Trump administration, but is skeptical Kinney could make a difference.   "How are you going to turn things around?" he asks, eyebrows raised.   
   "You need a person in there — that's me — who's a moderate who can talk to Republicans, who can talk to Democrats," she says. "I swear to you we're going to make a difference."   They chat for 10 minutes. At the end, he says he's actually already voted for her — but he's not optimistic.   "You have an uphill battle. This is the reddest state in the nation," he warns. "I applaud you — but there's a tsunami coming at you on the first Tuesday in November."   
   Mounting a run with little party infrastructure means no campaign office for Kinney, a former state senator. It means just a handful of "helpers" across the state and countless hours on the road to spread her message of preserving public lands and lowering health care costs.   "It's really tiring — but we have to see as many people as we can," she says. "If they can meet me, they feel more comfortable voting for me."   Rodney Lang, Kinney's husband, says a win for them is more than just the election day results.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A voter at a diner in Casper, Wyo., shows a photo of his ballot on his phone on Oct. 19, 2026, indicating he voted for Lisa Kinney.
                
                    Natalie Behring for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Natalie Behring for NPR
    

   
   "If we lose, the good news is the party's stronger, and we think we've contributed to that," he says.   Kinney calls herself a realist and says she knows many in the state will vote for whoever has an "R" next to their name.   "But I always have it in my mind that I can win," she adds.   'You can't just give it the ole college try'   Two thousand miles away, George Austin, a home builder and former football coach, says he feels a sense of kinship with Kinney.   "I applaud, I admire, I empathize, I commiserate with anyone and everyone who is in the same boat," he says.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                George Austin, 38, of Suffield, Conn., the Republican candidate for Connecticut's 2nd Congressional District, stands outside Enfield Town Hall in Enfield, Conn., on Oct. 30, 2026. Austin is challenging Democratic Rep. Joe Courtney, who has represented the largely Democratic district since 2007.
                
                    Christopher Capozziello for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Christopher Capozziello for NPR
    

   
   The pair are flip sides of the same coin; Kinney a speck of blue running in a red state, and Austin a Republican running in the Democratic stronghold of Connecticut.   
   They see up close a dynamic that has been brewing for some time — deep partisan entrenchment in states.   "In this Congress, there are 19 state delegations comprised of only representatives and senators from the same political party," said Eric Ostermeier, founder of the nonpartisan political news site Smart Politics. "That is a high watermark for nearly three quarters of a century — 1953 is the last time we saw numbers that high."   He says there's not just one reason for these "monolithic partisan tendencies."   
   Gerrymandering plays a role, diluting the voting strength of political minorities. But safe congressional seats are also produced without manipulation, with voters often sorting themselves geographically. Additionally, Ostermeier said it's difficult for state partisans to separate themselves from the national party identity.   "It's harder for a state office candidate to say, 'I'm a Wyoming Democrat, I'm not a Washington Democrat' — you get tainted by the national party," Ostermeier said.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Austin attends a trunk-or-treat Halloween event outside Enfield Town Hall in Enfield, Conn., on Oct. 30, 2026.
                
                    Christopher Capozziello for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Christopher Capozziello for NPR
    

   
   Austin has experienced that himself, with some voters quickly disengaging when they discover he's a Republican or once President Trump comes up in conversation.   "They ask me if I voted for him. I say, 'of course I did.' And we never get to discuss why," he says, adding there are areas where he disagrees with the administration.   He tries to steer conversations towards issues where there tends to be more common ground, like lamenting congressional gridlock, pushing for term limits, or placing guardrails on AI.   Austin is running to represent Connecticut's second congressional district, where the Democratic incumbent, Rep. Joe Courtney, has easily won reelection for 20 years. Democrats in the state have won 45 straight U.S. House elections since 2008.   "We haven't had any variety, any diversity in representation," Austin says. "I want to try to restore some balance."   He points to the high number of uncontested races in the state as another motivator.   
   "I want to win, I'm competitive and I believe in the cause — but that's the superficial motivation," Austin explained. "The nuanced one is that I want to be a catalyst to show other working men and women, other regular Joes out there, that this is worthwhile."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                George Austin decided to run for office because of what he saw as a lack of "diversity in representation."
                
                    Christopher Capozziello for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Christopher Capozziello for NPR
    

   
   Nationally, a significant share of state legislative seats are decided well ahead of Election Day because of the lack of competitive challengers. In Connecticut, 46 of the state legislature's 187 seats are uncontested.   
   Austin wears "many hats" in his campaign, including scheduler and volunteer coordinator. He also put a quarter of a million of his own money into the campaign, a sign of the financial toll these races can take.   "I'm successful, but I'm a far cry from wealthy — it's just what the people deserved, it's what the race deserved," he says.   He says it's important to run, even when the political odds are stacked against you.   "Word of caution — you really have to decide if you're in it for the right reasons because you're going to lose a whole bunch of sleep," he says. "It ain't for everyone, I'll tell you that right now. You can't just give it the ole college try – that's not what the race deserves, regardless of how outnumbered you are."   He acknowledges the path for a political minority like him — and Kinney — is challenging – but important.   "I definitely don't think that my race is a lost cause," he says. "But even if it was, you could argue that lost causes are the only ones worth fighting for."   Chris Polansky from Connecticut Public contributed reporting.

schema.headline: What's it like to run for Congress when the odds are stacked heavily against you?
